analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting striking workers' health insurance, with penalties up to $50,000 per violation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and got no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for an employer to terminate or significantly change a worker's employer-provided health insurance while the worker is on a lawful strike [S2]. Employers who violated the rule could face civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat violators, with possible personal liability for company officers who allowed it [S3]. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never advanced further before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who exercise their right to strike would keep their employer-provided health coverage during the strike, instead of facing a sudden loss of insurance for themselves and their families as a pressure tactic during contract negotiations [S2][S3]. Workers at companies with prior violations would get stronger penalties against repeat offenders [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It adds a new unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act: an employer may not terminate or significantly alter the health coverage of an employee while that employee is engaged in a lawful strike.

Violating employers face civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for employers with a repeat violation within five years, and individual directors or officers can be held personally liable if they directed, committed, or failed to prevent the violation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who could no longer cut health coverage as a strikebreaking tactic, and who could face civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubling to $100,000 for repeat violations within five years [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new costs on employers, including continued premium payments for striking workers and civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, doubling to $100,000 for repeat violators — a cost burden small employers would feel acutely.

The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to add a new unfair labor practice category, expanding the National Labor Relations Board's enforcement role and creating potential for litigation over what counts as 'significantly altering' coverage during a strike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to striking workers is direct and substantial: keeping employer health coverage during a strike removes one of the most coercive tools employers can use against a lawful walkout. The main cost is on employers, who must continue paying premiums during a strike and face new civil penalties; the bill offers no new help to employers who argue strikes are themselves costly. The penalty regime, doubling for repeat violations and reaching individual officers, is strong but was untested, and the bill as introduced did not address the separate problem of workers' plan coverage lapsing during long strikes for other reasons. On the whole, a plainly pro-worker measure with an honest cost to employers, and its death meant no change to the existing vulnerability.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 2, 2022, by Rep. Axne and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The House took no further action on the bill: no subcommittee or full committee vote, no floor debate, and no vote occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
All 42 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill had no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers retained the ability to cut health coverage for striking workers as a pressure tactic during negotiations, and no penalties or compliance costs were imposed on them. Striking workers remain exposed to losing health coverage mid-strike.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who can still cut strikers' coverage

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Axne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 42 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Cohen, Higgins (NY), Levin (MI), McGovern, Pascrell, Sanchez, and Williams (GA) as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred: no markup, no hearing on the record, and no vote to advance it.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill makes it an unfair labor practice to cut off or degrade health coverage for striking employees, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, so employers lose the option of using healthcare cutoffs as a strike tactic. For ordinary workers, health coverage during a strike is often the difference between striking and staying, so the employer interest here runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Insurers and plan sponsors would continue covering striking employees, adding administrative and cost considerations during strikes rather than being able to drop them.
